chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab from Ghiyath ibn Kalub from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Ja'far from his father (peace be upon them both) that 'Ali (peace be upon him) used to say:

"When a man marries a woman and has intercourse with her once, then turns away from her, she does not have the option [of khulu' or divorce] to wait, for she has been tried. And for the mothers of children and the concubines, if the husband has not been away from them for more than once, they do not have the option. As for what he mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him, of equating the case of 'unnah [impotence/delay] occurring after consummation with that occurring before consummation, he was led to do so by the generality of reports narrated regarding that, such as what he narrated."

key_terms.أُمَّهَاتِ الْأَوْلَادِ: Mothers of children, referring to wives who have borne children.
key_terms.الْخِيَارُ: The option/right to choose, specifically referring to the wife's right to initiate khulu' or separation.
key_terms.الْعُنَّةُ: Impotence or a condition preventing consummation or causing delay.
key_terms.اُبْتُلِيَتْ: She has been tried or tested, implying that the initial consummation validates the bond despite subsequent neglect.

ai.seo_question: Does a wife have the right to initiate divorce if her husband consummates the marriage once and then neglects her?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), narrating from Imam Ali (peace be upon him), clarifies the legal status of 'udhnah' (delay/neglect) in marriage, establishing that a single instance of non-consummation or neglect does not grant the wife unilateral khulu' rights, as she has already been 'tried' by the initial union. It further distinguishes between mothers of children and concubines, noting that the lack of option applies if the husband's absence has not exceeded a single instance, while scholars equate post-consummation and pre-consummation impotence based on the generality of reports. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that minor delays do not automatically trigger separation rights, preserving marital stability unless neglect becomes prolonged or habitual.
